Build comparison report — local LLM agent output, plus one frontier baseline

GoodDeal Build-Off

Three local models — run through the same coding agent and the same llama.cpp runtime — were each given the identical brief in prompt.md.txt: build a production-quality React + TypeScript + Tailwind landing page for a fictional deals platform called Good Deal, no template, no backend, must run after a plain install. A fourth build was added afterward from OpenAI Codex (GPT‑5.6) — a cloud/frontier model, not a local one — as a reference point for how far the local runs land from a current frontier baseline on the identical brief. Everything below was independently re-verified: builds run, TypeScript checked, all four apps rendered live in headless Chromium at three breakpoints, every listed interaction clicked through, and the DOM inspected before and after.

How this was verified

  • Build & typecheck — each project's own declared build script run from a clean install
  • Lint — each project's own declared lint script run as-is
  • Live render — all four dev servers launched and loaded in headless Chromium at 375px, 768px and 1440px
  • Console capture — page and console errors/warnings recorded on every load
  • Interaction testing — nav clicks, favorite toggle, countdown, newsletter submit driven programmatically and the DOM diffed before/after
  • Dependency audit — every package.json dependency grepped for actual usage in src/
  • Source review — every component read against the brief's 11 required sections and interaction list
  • Accessibility scan — heading order, aria-* usage, focus styling and alt text counted directly from source
  • Config audit — presence and correctness of tsconfig/Tailwind/PostCSS/ESLint config checked, not just assumed from a passing script name
  • Same brief, different runtime — Codex ran on OpenAI's cloud infrastructure rather than the local llama.cpp setup used for the other three; scored on the same rubric, but flagged throughout as not an apples-to-apples local comparison

Eight categories, weighted to the brief

Weights follow how much space the brief itself gives each concern — interactivity and page structure carry the most, since the prompt spends the most words on them. A ★ marks the highest score in each row.

02 — TECHNICAL SETUP & STACK COMPLIANCE

Three build clean. One doesn't build at all.

Empero7 / 10

React 19.2 + TypeScript 6 + Tailwind v4, plus react-router-dom, framer-motion, clsx and tailwind-merge. tsc -b && vite build finishes clean in 184ms.

All four extra packages are installed and sitting in node_modules but never imported anywhere in src/ — confirmed with a full-tree grep returning zero matches for each. That's a direct hit against the brief's own "avoid unused dependencies" line.

Ornith9 / 10

React 18.3 + TypeScript 5.6 + Tailwind v3. lucide-react is the only runtime dependency, and it's used throughout. Build finishes clean in 1.25s.

Every declared dependency is actually used. One rough edge: package.json wires up "lint": "eslint ." but eslint itself isn't in devDependencies, so npm run lint fails with eslint: not found. Dev, build and preview all run fine untouched.

Gemma1 / 10

No tsconfig.json, tailwind.config.js, postcss.config.js or ESLint config exist anywhere in the project — confirmed by a full directory listing. npm run build (tsc && vite build) exits 1 before touching a single file: with no tsconfig, tsc just prints its own --help text. npm run lint exits 2 with "ESLint couldn't find a configuration file."

Isolating vite build alone does technically finish in ~3.6s, but the shipped CSS is 90 bytes of un-transpiled @tailwind directives — with no postcss.config.js, the Tailwind pipeline never runs, so the "build" that does complete ships a completely unstyled site. This fails the brief's own top line: "must run successfully after installation without requiring manual fixes."

Codex9 / 10

React + TypeScript (strict: true) + Tailwind v3, with real tsconfig.json, tailwind.config.js, postcss.config.js and vite.config.ts all present and correct. tsc --noEmit && vite build is clean from a fresh rm -rf dist in ~1.5s. Confirmed the exact failure mode that broke Gemma doesn't apply here: dist/assets/*.css contains real compiled utility rules (.bg-ink{...}, .flex{...}), not raw @tailwind directives.

react, react-dom and lucide-react are the only dependencies, all three used. The one gap: there is no lint script at all and no ESLint config or dependency anywhere — npm run lint fails with "Missing script," functionally the same dead end as Ornith's broken one.

03 — DESIGN QUALITY & VISUAL CRAFT

Polished vs. art-directed

The brief explicitly warns against "generic AI-generated-looking layouts" and a repeated heading→subtitle→three-cards pattern. Both avoid the worst of it; only one takes a real compositional risk.

Empero11 / 15

Clean emerald/teal palette, generous whitespace, consistent card radii, soft blur-orb decoration. Product art is hand-built inline SVG data-URIs per deal — clever, zero network dependency — though visually crude (flat grey silhouettes with a text label baked in).

The hero itself is a centered headline over a search bar with three value-prop tiles beneath — a composition very close to the "generic SaaS landing page" template the brief asks to avoid.

Ornith14 / 15

The hero renders as a mock browser window holding four live deal tiles, paired with an asymmetric text column — a distinct, memorable composition. Sections vary deliberately: an off-center trust-metrics grid, a dark split-panel Deal of the Day, gradient-icon deal cards each with a different hue.

A consistent token system (brand-600, shadow-soft, a shared .card class) holds the whole page together without repeating the same card recipe everywhere.

Gemma1 / 15

Because Tailwind never compiles — in dev or prod — the rendered page is unstyled HTML: default blue underlined links, no backgrounds, no card borders or radii, no spacing, everything stacked top-to-bottom in browser-default black-on-white. Confirmed with getComputedStyle: a category icon's background-color returns rgba(0,0,0,0) before and after hover, though the source class is bg-indigo-100 hover:bg-indigo-600.

The brief's "Important Visual Challenge" — vary composition instead of repeating heading→subtitle→cards — may be intended in the JSX (an asymmetric hero block, a split Deal-of-the-Day layout), but none of it is visible in the rendered output. There is currently no design to assess beyond default browser typography.

Codex14.5 / 15

A genuine custom design system: a five-color palette (ink, moss, mint, citrus, coral) defined in tailwind.config.js, consistent spacing rhythm, and heavy display type. Composition varies deliberately across sections — an asymmetric floating-card hero, a 4-col trending grid with one 2-col spotlight card, a full-bleed dark Deal of the Day panel, a big colored block paired with a 2×2 metric grid for trust stats instead of four identical tiles.

One real ding against "sufficient color contrast": the coral CTA color (#FF6B4A) paired with white text — used on 5 of the page's most prominent buttons, including "Find Deals" and "Create Alert" — measures 2.82:1, failing WCAG AA for both normal and large text.

04 — PAGE STRUCTURE COMPLETENESS

All 11 required sections, every time

Empero13.5 / 15

Header, hero, categories, trending deals, deal of the day, how-it-works, store logos, trust stats, testimonials, newsletter, footer — every section present, nothing left as a placeholder.

The store strip names real retailers — Amazon, Best Buy, Target, Walmart, Newegg, eBay — as plain text behind colored emoji circles. No copyrighted logo assets are used, but the brief specifically asks for "fictional or generic" partner stores.

Ornith14.5 / 15

Same full set of 11 sections, each mapped to a real in-page anchor id (#deals, #categories, #stores, #how-it-works) rather than existing only visually.

Partner stores are entirely invented — SoundLab, PixelForge, Stride, KeyWorks, Wanderly, VitalFit — each with an initials monogram. A closer, safer read of "fictional or generic."

Gemma11 / 15

All 11 required sections are present in LandingPage.tsx's composition — header, hero, categories, trending deals, deal of the day, how-it-works, store logos + trust metrics, testimonials, newsletter, footer — none left as a placeholder in markup terms.

Two rough edges: the header's "Deals" and "Categories" nav items both point at the identical #categories anchor, with no separate target for trending deals — and because nothing renders visibly styled (see §03), the section-to-section visual variation the brief also asks for can't be assessed as delivered, only as coded.

Codex15 / 15

All 11 sections present and correctly ordered — header, hero, categories, 6 trending deal cards (meeting the brief's "at least 6"), deal of the day, three-step how-it-works, 8 fictional store names, trust stats (50K+/12K+/500+/$2M+), 3 testimonials with avatar/name/role, newsletter, and a footer with product/company/resources link groups plus social icons and legal links.

No structural gaps found — no real-brand names standing in for the fictional store strip, no placeholder copy left in, and the "at least 6 deal cards" minimum is met exactly at 6 with one visually promoted as a spotlight card rather than treated identically to the rest.

05 — INTERACTIVITY & FUNCTIONAL CORRECTNESS

The category that decides the report

Every required interaction was driven live in headless Chromium — clicked, filled, submitted — and the DOM was diffed before and after, not just read from source.

Empero8 / 20

Mobile nav toggle, hover states and the countdown timer all work exactly as coded. Three of the eight required interactions do not:

Favorite button — clicking the heart updates a favorites Set inside App.tsx, but that state is never passed down to TrendingDeals/DealCard. DealCard reads deal.isFavorite straight off the static mock data instead, so the icon never changes. Verified: heart's CSS class was byte-identical before and after a real click.

Newsletter errors — validateEmail() correctly flags a bad address, but the failure branch only calls setErrorMessage() — it never calls setStatus('error'), and the red border/error text are gated on status === 'error'. Invalid emails submit in total silence. Verified live with two different malformed addresses.

Header navigation — "Deals / Categories / Stores / How It Works" call window.location.href = '/deals' — a hard navigation to routes that don't exist. react-router-dom is installed but never wired up; this only "works" in dev because Vite's SPA fallback re-serves index.html. On a plain static host it would 404.

Ornith18 / 20

Every required interaction fired correctly under live testing:

Favorite button — toggles instantly; aria-label flips from "Add deal to favorites" to "Remove deal from favorites" and the fill/background classes update in the same click. Verified via DOM diff.

Newsletter — a malformed address produces an immediate red role="alert" message; a valid address shows a personalized role="status" success message after a simulated 900ms delay. Both verified live.

Navigation — nav links are real in-page anchors; clicking "Deals" scrolled the page (confirmed scrollY change) with no reload, backed by scroll-behavior: smooth.

Two points held back: category cards link to #deals rather than implementing a persisted "selected" filter state (Empero has the same gap), and a stray if (status === 'success') reset() line in the submit handler reads a stale closure value — harmless, but confused logic.

Gemma5 / 20

Only three interactions hold up live: mobile nav toggle (icon and aria-label correctly flip), the newsletter's success path (a real 1500ms delay then a genuine success message), and header nav scrolling via plain CSS scroll-behavior: smooth (confirmed via a real scrollY change).

Favorite button — DealCard.tsx's heart button has no onClick and no state at all; outerHTML captured before and after a live click is byte-identical. Countdown timer — DealOfTheDay.tsx computes a correct 72-hour endTime but then renders <CountdownTimer endTime={new Date()} />, passing "now" instead — the page shows "Deal Expired!" at first paint and is unchanged 3 seconds later, live-verified. Category selection doesn't exist as a feature — no click handler or selected state anywhere in DealCategories.tsx.

Newsletter validation — the input is type="email" with no noValidate, so a plainly invalid string like "not-an-email" is intercepted by the browser's own popup before React's custom error branch ever runs; the app's designed AlertTriangle error UI was unreachable in this test.

Codex19 / 20

Every required interaction fired correctly under live DOM-diff testing. Mobile nav — opens, scrolls to the target section on a link click, and closes itself. Category selection — clicking a category flips aria-pressed "false"→"true" and swaps the visible style. Favorite — aria-label and aria-pressed both flip and the heart icon's fill class genuinely changes, verified via literal DOM diff. Countdown — a real setInterval against a fixed future target actually ticked down across two live reads 2.2s apart.

Newsletter — the form sets noValidate so invalid input reaches React's own logic instead of a native popup — "not-an-email" produces a custom message and aria-invalid="true"; a valid address produces a distinctly styled success message. Nav links — real scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'}) calls, confirmed via scrollY change. One point held back: like Ornith, it's unconfirmed whether selecting a category actually filters the visible deal list or only changes the button's own state.

EXHIBIT C — newsletter form after submitting an invalid address, captured live
06 — RESPONSIVE BEHAVIOR

375 / 768 / 1440 — two render correctly, one never responds at all

Empero8 / 10

Renders correctly at all three breakpoints with no overflow or broken layout. Category grid steps 2 → 3 → 6 columns, deal cards step 1 → 2 → 3, and the mobile menu collapses properly. The same 1 → 2 → 3 step is reused for most grids on the page.

Ornith8.5 / 10

Same clean coverage at all three breakpoints. The hero's four-tile browser mockup deliberately stays a 2×2 grid on mobile instead of collapsing to a single column, which reads as a considered per-section decision rather than one grid rule applied everywhere.

Gemma1 / 10

Responsive behavior does not run at all: grid-template-columns measured via getComputedStyle on both the categories grid and the trending-deals grid returns "none" at 768px and 375px alike — display: grid itself never applies, at any width, because the Tailwind classes generating it were never compiled.

Worse than a naive stack: the header's hidden md:flex desktop nav and md:hidden mobile hamburger are both simultaneously visible at every viewport, including 1440px — confirmed in the 1440px screenshot, where the full desktop nav, both search inputs and the hamburger icon all render at once. No horizontal overflow occurs, but only because the page has no layout at all to overflow.

Codex9.5 / 10

The only build where responsive grids were verified numerically, not just visually: getComputedStyle().gridTemplateColumns shows the trending-deals grid actually resolving 4 columns at 1440px → 2 at 768px → 1 at 375px, and the categories grid 6 → 3 → 2 — both matching their source lg:/md:/sm: classes exactly.

The header collapses through three distinct breakpoints rather than one crude toggle, and scrollWidth vs clientWidth confirmed zero horizontal overflow at both 768px and 375px.

07 — ACCESSIBILITY

Semantics were a constraint for one build, an afterthought for the other

Empero5 / 10

Heading order is clean (h1 → h2 → h3 → h4). Only 7 aria-* attributes exist across the entire app, and the mobile menu toggle has no aria-expanded/aria-controls.

Just 4 custom focus: classes in the whole codebase, all on the newsletter input — every button falls back to the browser's default focus ring rather than a designed state. The two real <img> elements do carry alt text.

Ornith9 / 10

17 aria-* attributes, including aria-expanded/aria-controls on the mobile toggle and a dynamic aria-label on every icon-only button. The newsletter's two feedback states use role="status" and role="alert" correctly.

A shared Button component plus a base .btn class bakes a focus-visible ring into every interactive control site-wide, rather than needing it re-added per button. No <img> elements exist at all — product art is an icon-on-gradient tile — so alt text is sidestepped rather than solved, noted but not penalized.

Gemma3 / 10

Just 3 aria-* attributes exist in the entire codebase (hamburger aria-label, a static "Add to favorites" label, and templated social-icon labels) — thinner than either other build. The mobile menu toggle has no aria-expanded/aria-controls despite controlling a collapsible panel.

18 focus: classes exist but zero use focus-visible:, and several interactive elements (category cards, testimonial avatar, footer links) carry no custom focus styling at all. Heading order also skips a level: the footer jumps from the page's h2 sections straight to an h4 brand heading with no h3 between. The single <img> in the app does carry correct alt text.

Codex7.5 / 10

The deepest aria coverage of the four: 31 aria-* attributes (18 aria-hidden, 6 aria-label, plus aria-pressed, aria-expanded/aria-controls, aria-describedby, aria-invalid, aria-live), 15 distinct focus-visible:outline applications, and a clean heading order with no skipped level.

Set against that: a real, measured contrast failure. The coral-on-white CTA color used on 5 prominent buttons — including "Find Deals" and "Create Alert" — computes to 2.82:1, failing WCAG AA (needs 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large). The brief explicitly asks for "sufficient color contrast," and this lands on the page's own primary conversion buttons.

08 — CODE QUALITY & ARCHITECTURE

Split into components vs. actually decomposed

Empero8 / 15

11 components plus types.ts and data.ts — reasonable single-responsibility split on the surface. But the favorite-button bug is a direct symptom of state that was never actually threaded between App and the card grid, and the newsletter bug is the same kind of gap.

Four unused dependencies (see §02) bloat the install. Two lint warnings for unnecessary escape characters in data.ts. No test runner configured.

Ornith13 / 15

Deliberately layered: Layout/, sections/, ui/, hooks/, data/. Stateful logic is pulled out into useCountdown and useNewsletter hooks instead of living inside the components that render it — genuinely reusable, and it's why the interactions actually work end to end.

vitest is wired into package.json as a test runner, though no test files were actually written — a smaller version of the same "declared but unused" pattern, and the lint script itself is broken (see §02).

Gemma4 / 15

A flat, sensible-looking split — 10 components plus a types.ts and data/mockData.ts — but it doesn't hold up under a typecheck. Copying src/ into a standard Vite+TS config and running tsc --noEmit surfaces 5 real compile errors independent of the missing-config problem: HeroSection.tsx imports a nonexistent ./ui/Button (TS2307) and then defines a redundant local Button as an unused fallback; mockData.ts references NewsletterFormState without importing it (TS2304); and a local Check SVG helper is called with an invalid size prop three times (TS2322).

6+ unused imports across DealCard.tsx, HeroSection.tsx, SocialProof.tsx, Testimonials.tsx, mockData.ts and LandingPage.tsx. No test runner is configured and no test files exist.

Codex10 / 15

Clean, strictly-typed code — 14 logically separate components (Header, Hero, DealCard, TrendingDeals, DealOfTheDay, etc.) with typed props throughout — but every one of them lives inside a single 693-line App.tsx rather than a components/ folder, short of the "modern component-based architecture" the brief's phrasing implies at the file level. Mock data is properly separated into src/data/deals.ts with typed interfaces.

Zero unused runtime dependencies, but one unused import (Watch from lucide-react, deals.ts:16), and — as in §02 — no lint tooling configured at all, so no automated quality check ran over this code before shipping it. No tests configured or written.

09 — FINAL VALIDATION & CONSOLE HYGIENE

A clean build log isn't the same as a working app

Empero4 / 5

tsc -b && vite build is clean; zero console errors or warnings at any of the three breakpoints. But the brief's own closing checklist asks the builder to "verify all interactive elements work" — the favorite button and the newsletter's error state are broken silently, with no console trace. That's precisely the class of defect a clean build log won't catch.

Ornith4.5 / 5

tsc -b && vite build is clean; zero console errors or warnings at any breakpoint. Unlike Empero, the interactive elements were actually exercised and matched their coded intent in every case tested. Half a point held back for the broken lint script.

Gemma0.5 / 5

npm run build fails (exit 1), npm run lint fails (exit 2), and npm run preview serves an HTTP 404 since no dist/ was ever produced. Of the brief's own closing checklist — build succeeds, no TypeScript errors, no console errors — only "no runtime console errors" holds: the rendered (if unstyled) page throws no console errors or warnings once the dev server is loaded directly, which is the only reason this category isn't a flat zero.

Codex4 / 5

tsc --noEmit && vite build is clean from a fresh rm -rf dist, and every interactive element matched its coded intent under live testing. One genuine miss on the brief's own "check for console errors" step: index.html has no <link rel="icon">, so the browser's automatic favicon request throws a real 404 console error on every load at 1440px (0 errors at 768px/375px, where the automatic request behaves differently). Small, but it's a literal console error the brief's checklist asks to catch.

10 — VERIFIED DEFECT LEDGER

Eighteen concrete findings, all reproduced live

Sev.BuildDefectVerification
11 — VERDICT

Ornith still wins — but a frontier model closes most of the gap Gemma opened

Among the three local builds, Empero and Ornith both install cleanly, build with zero TypeScript errors, and throw no console errors — on that surface they look like a tie. The gap between them opens the moment the page is actually used: Ornith's build passes every required interaction tested live — favoriting, the countdown, both newsletter states, and real in-page navigation — while Empero ships two interactions that are silently dead (the favorite button and newsletter error state) and a navigation scheme that only works by accident of Vite's dev-server fallback. Gemma doesn't reach that conversation at all — no config files exist at all, npm run build and npm run lint both fail immediately, and Tailwind never compiles even in dev, so the page renders as unstyled default HTML with a favorite button and countdown timer that are both dead code. That's the brief's own opening line, "must run successfully after installation without requiring manual fixes," failing outright.

Codex — a frontier cloud model, not a local one, added afterward as a reference point — is the closest thing to a clean sweep of the four, finishing at 88.5/100, just behind Ornith's 90.5. Every required interaction actually works, verified live: a favorite toggle with a real DOM/aria diff, a countdown genuinely ticking down from a fixed future target, category selection with real state feedback, newsletter validation that correctly uses noValidate so its own custom error UI runs instead of a native popup, and responsive grids confirmed numerically to resolve 4→2→1 and 6→3→2 columns across breakpoints. It also ships the most art-directed design of the four, with a real custom color system and deliberately varied section composition.

What keeps Codex from taking the top spot: a measured, brief-violating contrast failure (2.82:1) on five of its own primary CTA buttons, no lint tooling configured at all, all 14 components living in a single 693-line file rather than a proper components/ structure, and one console error on load from a missing favicon. Ornith's remaining edge is narrower engineering discipline — logic pulled into hooks, a layered folder structure, denser accessibility coverage with no contrast defects — even though its lint script is just as broken as Codex's missing one.

Worth flagging The three local models ran at the same Q8_0 quantization, so quant level isn't a confound among them — the quality gap traces back to base model/training, not precision loss. Codex is a genuinely different kind of comparison: a much larger, closed, cloud-hosted frontier model run through a different agent/runtime than the local llama.cpp setup, added specifically to answer "how far behind is local, really?" rather than to compete head-to-head on equal footing. Treat its score as an upper-bound reference point, not a same-class result — and treat all four numbers as one prompt run once per model, not a controlled study.
Assessed against prompt.md.txt — same brief throughout; three local checkpoints on the same agent/llama.cpp runtime, plus one frontier cloud model (Codex) on a different runtime for reference. Verification: build + typecheck + live Chromium render + DOM-level interaction diff
